title: Share a short spoken report
intro: I can choose one topic, put my ideas in order and share them so my listeners can follow.
example: Kai reports a discovery: “Our bean seed changed. First, a white root appeared. Next, two green leaves opened.” The first sentence names the topic. Both details explain the same discovery, and first and next show the order. Kai rehearses with a partner, faces the group and uses a voice they can hear comfortably.
steps: 1. Choose a topic and relevant details
A report tells listeners about an idea or event. Name one topic first, then select details that explain it. A true fact can still be unrelated to this report.
Topic: our classroom snail. Possible details: it left a shiny trail; it has a shell; my shoes are blue.
Which two details help your classmates learn about the snail?
The shiny trail and shell describe the snail. Blue shoes do not explain this topic. An opening could be “We watched our classroom snail.”
2. Put the ideas in order
Use first and next when events have an order. A small prompt can remind you of an idea without containing every word. Tell a connected sentence for each prompt.
Adult: draw three simple cards now: an empty pot, a hand planting a seed, a pot with a shoot. Display them in that order. Say the names of the pictures together.
Use the three pictures to tell what happened.

For example: “First we had an empty pot. Next we planted a seed. Later a shoot grew.” Accept another accurate connected report. The actual drawings are memory cues; the child supplies the spoken sentences.
3. Rehearse for your listeners
Try the report with one person. Ask whether they heard it and understood the order. Face the group and adjust your volume for the room. Clear does not mean shouting.
Mina whispers her report and a partner cannot hear the last detail. The topic and order are clear.
What could Mina change before sharing with a small group?
Rehearse the final detail with a comfortably stronger voice while facing the listeners. Pause between ideas and check whether the group can hear. Keep the same relevant ideas.
mistakes: “A report needs every fact I know.”
Choose details that explain the one topic.
“Louder is always clearer.”
Use a comfortable volume that reaches the listeners.
“A prompt must show every word.”
A small picture can remind you of an idea; say the sentence yourself.
activity: Choose something you really noticed today. Name the topic, draw two detail prompts and put them in order. Rehearse with an adult, then share with a willing partner or small group. Ask what they learnt from your report.
adjust: Starter: choose between two relevant details with an adult. Core: give an opening and two ordered details. Stretch: answer one on-topic listener question and add a useful detail.
safety: Use speech, sign or AAC with suitable support. Record topic and order separately from actual voice volume; a written answer cannot demonstrate spoken delivery. Do not require a child to share private experiences.
tricky: 1. “My seed grew. I like chips.” Is this a focused report?
The seed sentence fits the topic; chips do not explain the seed. Add a detail such as its new leaves.
2. Can a report share a response to a story?

Yes. First supply the text event: “Niko found his lost boot and could go home.” A report might be “I felt relieved when Niko found his boot because he could go home.” The reason connects the response to that event.
3. Does reading a script show the same skill as using picture prompts?
It can support sharing, but it does not show that the speaker can expand picture prompts into their own connected report. Notice the support used.
faq: How long should a report be?
Use a short, manageable turn with one topic and a few relevant ideas. There is no compulsory time limit here.
What should an adult notice?
Listen for a clear topic, relevant ordered details and communication that the actual audience can follow. Check voice volume through a real speaking turn where appropriate.

title: Form letters with a taught movement
intro: I can watch where a letter starts, follow its movement and check the letter I make.
example: Adult: place your school’s approved lower-case c and upper-case T models on paper. Demonstrate each complete letter once, then slowly repeat its actual start and stroke direction. The learner sky-writes the movement, traces the model and makes a fresh copy. Compare the new copy with the demonstrated shape, size and orientation; the printed samples below identify letters but do not prescribe a school handwriting script.
steps: 1. Watch the starting point and direction
Watch the whole letter first. Then notice where each stroke begins and the route it follows. A recognisable finished shape does not tell us which movement the writer used.
Adult: draw the school-approved lower-case c with a start dot and direction arrow. Demonstrate the movement aloud. Provide blank paper beside this actual model.
Point to the start, sky-write the movement, then make your own c.
Check the learner against the supplied school model: the same starting point and direction, a recognisable curved shape and an open right side. Demonstrate again if the movement is uncertain.
2. Place each form on writing guides
Use the writing guides taught at school. Compare a lower-case form with its upper-case partner; the capital may have a different shape, not just a larger size.
Adult: draw the school’s writing guides and model lower-case t and upper-case T on them, with their taught starts and stroke order. Leave a blank pair of guides.
Form t and T on the blank guides. What will you compare?
Compare each letter with its own model for start, movement, height, placement and orientation. Do not enlarge lower-case t and call it the capital; use the taught T form.
3. Write and check with a comfortable hand

A functional grip lets the pencil move with control and without pain or excessive effort. Try a short writing turn, pause and compare one letter before writing more. Formation is different from naming a letter.
Adult: demonstrate the school-approved n, then cover the model after a supported trace. Invite one fresh n on paper. Ask about hand comfort.
How can you check the letter and your hand?

Uncover the model and compare the start, direction and recognisable form. Ask whether the hand feels comfortable. Adjust paper angle, tool or support if needed; do not force one identical grip for every learner.
mistakes: “If it looks close, the movement does not matter.”
Follow the taught start and direction to build a reliable movement.
“Pressing harder improves every letter.”
Use enough pressure to make a clear mark without strain.
“Naming a letter proves I can form it.”
Watch the actual writing movement and inspect the new letter.
activity: An adult selects one curved, one straight and one slanting letter from the school model, demonstrates each and supplies a practice line. Sky-write, trace, make a fresh copy and compare. Return to another small set later so both cases across the alphabet are taught over time.
adjust: Starter: a large movement and one trace. Core: form a fresh letter on guides after the model. Stretch: form a taught upper/lower-case pair from a named prompt, then compare each with the model.
safety: Provide accessible tools and short turns. Stop if writing hurts and seek suitable school support. A typed answer, selected glyph or static sample does not demonstrate pencil movement.
tricky: 1. Must every child hold a pencil in exactly the same way?
No. Aim for a comfortable, functional grip that supports controlled movement.
2. Is a large a automatically an upper-case A?
No. A and a have distinct taught forms. Compare each with the correct case model.
3. Can you learn every letter by copying c’s movement?
No. Letters use different movements. Follow the actual taught model for each letter, revisiting both cases across sessions.
faq: Which handwriting style should we use?
Use the school’s approved style consistently. This page supports observing and following it; ordinary screen fonts are identification samples.
What counts as evidence of formation?
An observed writing turn and the learner’s fresh letters. Note any tracing, start dots, demonstrations or physical support supplied.

title: Listen for patterns in spoken words
intro: I can hear and make rhymes, repeated beginnings and word beats, then notice a smaller speech sound.
example: Adult: say “boat, goat” and “busy bee” naturally before showing print. Boat and goat rhyme because their spoken endings match. Busy bee repeats its beginning sound, so it shows alliteration. Now say “rabbit”: two claps mark its two syllables. Say “moon” and hold its first humming sound: that is one phoneme, smaller than a syllable.
steps: 1. Hear and make a rhyme
Listen from the vowel to the end of the spoken word. Rhymes share that ending sound. Print can help an adult remember the words, but the child should decide by listening.
Adult: say “hen, pen, dog”. Repeat each whole word. Keep the written words out of the child’s view.
Which word does not rhyme with the other two? Say another rhyme for hen.
Dog is different. Hen and pen rhyme; ten or another matching spoken rhyme can join them. Accept a valid rhyme in the child’s variety of English.
2. Repeat the beginning sound
Alliteration repeats the first speech sound of nearby words. It is not the same as sharing any letter or having a matching ending. Say each word aloud.
Adult: say “Sam sees seals” and “Sam likes jam”. Repeat the beginning of each word gently.
Which phrase repeats the same beginning sound? Make another matching pair.
Sam sees seals repeats the hissing beginning sound. “Silly snake” is another possible pair. Sam and jam rhyme, but their first sounds differ.
3. Hear beats, then isolate one sound
A syllable is a spoken beat. A phoneme is an individual speech sound. Clap the beats in a whole word, then listen for a specified smaller sound without reciting letter names.
Adult: say “sun”, then “rabbit”. Clap their beats. Say “sun” again and model its first hissing sound without an extra “uh”.
How many beats are in each word? What sound starts sun?

Sun has one syllable; rabbit usually has two. Sun begins with the hissing sound /s/. Its one syllable contains three phonemes. The child imitates the heard sound; reading this notation is not required.
mistakes: “Rhyme means the first sounds match.”
Compare the spoken endings; matching beginnings make alliteration.
“One clap always means one sound.”
A clap marks a syllable, which may contain several speech sounds.
“The letter name is the sound I heard.”
Say the cue word and imitate the specified speech sound.
activity: An adult says “cat, hat, fish” for a rhyme choice; asks for a new rhyme for cat; then says “Mia makes maps” for a beginning-sound pattern. Finish by clapping banana and isolating the first sound of fish. Keep the activity oral and let the child repeat words.
adjust: Starter: choose a rhyme from two spoken words. Core: generate a rhyme and an alliterative pair, then clap beats. Stretch: explain why dog has one beat but three phonemes and isolate its final sound.
safety: Use familiar words and the child’s natural pronunciation. Adults supply real speech; silent print is not an audio test. Accept a pointed choice for recognition while separately observing spoken generation if that is the goal.
tricky: 1. Do blue and shoe rhyme even though their spellings differ?
Yes, their spoken endings match in usual Australian pronunciation. Listen rather than compare letters.
2. Do cat and kite show alliteration?
Yes, they begin with the same /k/ sound, although their first letters differ. They do not rhyme.
3. Is banana three words because it has three claps?
No. Banana is one word with three syllables. The claps do not separate it into three meaning units.
faq: Must every rhyme be a real word?
Playful invented rhymes can practise the sound pattern. Ask separately for a real word when that is the goal.
What if a word has a different beat count in a child’s pronunciation?
Listen to their natural spoken form and discuss it respectfully. Do not mark a dialect difference as a listening error.

title: Break up, blend and change spoken sounds
intro: I can hear words in a sentence, blend and separate sounds, and change a sound to make a new word.
exampleTitle: Add, remove or replace one sound
example: Keep this oral. Adult: say “at”, then add the humming beginning sound of moon at the start: “mat”. Remove that added sound to return to “at”. Say “mat” again and replace its last sound with the beginning sound of pig: “map”. Use a counter for each heard sound; show which counter is added, removed or replaced while the others stay in order.
steps: 1. Separate a sentence into words
Say the whole sentence. Repeat it and move one counter for every word, including short words. A word may have more than one syllable, so clapping beats is a different task.
Adult: say “My raincoat is wet.” Repeat naturally, then slowly.
Move one counter per word. How many words are there?
Four: My | raincoat | is | wet. Raincoat has two syllables but is one word in this sentence. Say the whole sentence again after counting.
2. Blend and segment a single-syllable word
For blending, listen to each supplied speech sound in order and join them smoothly. For segmenting, begin with a whole spoken word and separate its sounds. Avoid adding “uh” to consonants.
Adult: supply /s/ /ʌ/ /n/ using sun, up and nest as cues. Then say “ship” as a whole word. Keep printed spellings hidden from the child.
Blend the first sounds. Then move a counter for each sound in ship.
The first sequence makes sun. Ship has three sounds: /ʃ/ /ɪ/ /p/. The sh sound uses one counter even though adults spell it with two letters. These are sound tasks, not letter counting.
3. Change just the named sound
First say the starting word and identify the sound position. Add a counter for an added sound, take one away for deletion or swap one for substitution. Reblend and check that the other sounds stayed.
Adult: say “lip”; add the beginning sound of sun at the start. Say “best”; remove its /s/. Say “pin”; replace its middle vowel with the vowel in pen.
Say the three new words. What operation made each one?
Slip adds initial /s/; bet removes /s/ from best; pen replaces the middle vowel in pin. The other sounds remain in the same order. Work on one operation at a time before mixing them.
mistakes: “A long word must count as several words.”
Count whole words in the sentence separately from their syllables.
“Each written letter needs one sound counter.”
In an oral task, counters stand for heard sounds, including one for sh in ship.
“Change a sound means replace the whole word.”
Keep the unchanged sound counters in place and alter only the named position.
activity: Adult: say “tea” and add /m/, the beginning sound of moon, at the end to make team. Say “smile” and remove its first /s/ to make mile. Say “mop” and replace its first /m/ with /t/ to make top. Let the learner move counters and say each result before you reveal it.
adjust: Starter: blend two sounds and add an initial sound to at. Core: blend and segment three sounds, then add, delete and replace a specified sound. Stretch: start with cap and insert /l/ after /k/ to make clap, explaining which position was added.
safety: Use familiar words and local pronunciation; teacher sound notation is not child reading material. Work orally with real adult speech. A counter diagram cannot certify hearing or pronunciation. Separate speech-production support from sound-awareness observations.
tricky: 1. Can one-syllable frog have four phonemes?
Yes: /f/ /r/ /ɒ/ /g/. Syllables and individual speech sounds measure different parts of speech.
2. Change the final /p/ in cheap to /t/. Is the new word cheat?
Yes. Keep the initial ch sound and long vowel. Only the final phoneme changes; spelling is not the task.
3. Add /l/ after /k/ in cap. Is this a replacement?
No. It is an insertion: cap becomes clap. There are now four phonemes rather than three.
faq: Should the child see printed words?
Keep print hidden for these listening tasks. The adult-facing words and notation specify what to say accurately.
How do we check the whole code?

Across short sessions, observe sentence-to-word segmentation, oral blending and segmentation, isolation, and addition, deletion and substitution at suitable sound positions. One successful change is only one piece of evidence.

title: Know letter names, forms and common sounds
intro: I can recognise and name both case forms and connect a letter with a commonly taught sound.
exampleTitle: One letter identity, two printed forms
example: M and m look different but both have the letter name em. Their common sound is the humming beginning of moon, not the spoken name em. The table below keeps case, name and cue separate for all 26 letters. Use a few at a time in mixed order, then return to the others across sessions.
steps: 1. Match and name the two forms
Look at the actual printed letter, find its case partner and say their shared name. Recognising a letter in mixed order is different from singing the alphabet sequence.
Printed choices: B, d, D, b.
Make two case pairs and name each pair.
B pairs with b, named bee. D pairs with d, named dee. Case changes the form, not the letter identity. Trace a distinguishing shape feature if b and d are confused.
2. Separate a name from a common sound
A name identifies a letter. A sound is what the letter can represent in a word. Say a familiar cue word, then isolate the relevant sound. A letter may represent other sounds in other words.
Printed P p. Name: pee. Cue: pet. Printed C c. Name: see. Cue: cup.
What common sound does each cue teach?
P/p represents the first sound /p/ in pet; C/c represents /k/ in cup. Neither answer is the letter name. Do not add an extra vowel after the consonant or claim c always represents /k/.
3. Find a known letter inside a word
Connect the printed form with its name and a common sound, then apply it in a familiar word. A name card is useful for recognition, but not every personal name follows simple sound patterns.
Printed word: mat. Adult: model /m/ /æ/ /t/ and blend mat. Point to m, then show M.
Which letter names both forms, and which sound helps read mat?
Both forms are em; /m/, the humming beginning of moon, helps read mat. Say the sounds and blend them, rather than blending the alphabet names em, ay, tee.
mistakes: “Upper-case and lower-case are different letters.”
Match the forms by their shared name.
“Saying pee answers the sound question.”
Pee is the name; give the first sound of pet for this common association.
“Every letter always means one sound.”
Letters can work in teams or have different sounds in different words. Explain x and qu carefully.
activity: Make cards for five taught letters in both cases. Mix them, find partners and name each letter. An adult then asks separately for a common sound using the reference cues. Locate one of these letters in a meaningful label or a learner’s preferred printed name.
adjust: Starter: match one upper-case card to two lower-case choices. Core: name mixed-case letters and give separate common sounds. Stretch: recognise a previously taught form inside a word and explain how it helps with blending. Revisit the full alphabet over later sessions.
safety: Accept conventional local letter-name variants. A selected answer may show recognition but does not demonstrate oral naming. Ask the child to say or communicate each name and sound separately, with suitable access support.
tricky: 1. Does x in fox represent only one phoneme?
No. Final x here represents /k/ followed by /s/: two phonemes. Its letter name is ex.
2. Does q by itself always represent two sounds?
No. In queen, teach the printed team qu with /k/ followed by /w/. Do not attribute the whole team’s sounds to isolated q in every word.
3. Is y’s name why the sound we blend at the start of yes?
No. Why is the letter name. The first sound of yes is the common consonant association used here.
faq: Does this table list every sound a letter can represent?
No. It supplies a common early association. Read each cue naturally and teach further correspondences through a systematic school sequence.
Does matching a few pairs show the whole alphabet is secure?
No. Sample both cases in mixed order across sessions. Record recognition, naming and common-sound association separately for all 26 letters.

title: Read and write CVC words
intro: I can use taught letter sounds to read a CVC word and write each sound in order.
exampleTitle: Hear hen; write hen; read it back
example: Adult: say “hen” without showing the spelling. The learner repeats it and moves three sound counters. Write h for the first sound, e for the short middle vowel and n for the final sound. Then show the completed word, point under each letter and blend hen. For reading, begin with the printed letters; for spelling, begin with the spoken word.
steps: 1. Blend the printed word
Point from left to right. Say the taught sound linked to each letter and join the sounds smoothly. Check that the whole word makes sense; do not guess from a picture or the first letter.
Printed word: map. Taught cues: moon beginning for m, apple beginning for a, pig beginning for p.
Read the word. How did you check all three positions?
/m/ /æ/ /p/ blend to map. Touch each printed letter in order. The word names something that shows places; meaning confirms the blended reading.
2. Map a spoken word into letters
Listen to the whole word, segment its sounds and choose a taught letter for every position. The middle vowel must be represented as well as the consonants.
Adult: say “bed” without displaying it. Supply blank paper and taught letter cards b, e, d, a, t.
Write the word you heard, then read it back.
Bed: b, e, d in order. Use three counters if needed. If a sound is missing, say the word again and locate the empty sound position before choosing its letter.
3. Change one position and reread
Change only the named letter, use its sound and blend the whole new word. Compare first, middle and final positions instead of guessing that the word stayed the same.
Printed word: sit. Replace i with a to make sat. Then replace s with m.
Read the last word. Which positions changed in each step?
The last word is mat. Sit to sat changes the middle vowel; sat to mat changes the first consonant. The other two positions stay fixed at each step. Read all three letters after each change.
mistakes: “The first letter is enough.”
Read every position and blend the whole word.
“The vowel can be left out.”
Stretch the word and listen to the middle sound.
“Letter names blend into the word.”
Use the sounds associated with the printed letters.
activity: Adult: say “dog” for writing without showing it. Then show the different word “cup” for reading. Ask the learner to point to all positions and explain any repair. Keep the two tasks separate so a displayed word does not give away the spelling answer.
adjust: Starter: two of three letter positions supplied with counters. Core: spell a spoken CVC word and blend a different printed word. Stretch: explain why hn cannot fully spell hen, then repair it and read the whole word.
safety: Use previously taught correspondences and familiar vocabulary. An adult supplies actual dictated speech. Copying a visible spelling is supported practice, not independent spelling from sound.
tricky: 1. A child writes hn for hen. Is the final sound missing?
No. The final n is present. The middle vowel e is missing.
2. Can the letters in map be rearranged freely?
No. Sound order matters. Map and pam have different sequences; use the intended whole word as your check.
3. Is every three-letter word a simple CVC word?
No. The pattern concerns consonant–vowel–consonant sounds and their taught spellings. Use simple examples such as cat, bed, sit, dog and sun here.
faq: Must a child name a picture before reading?
No. For reading, show the word and blend its letters first. Use a picture or explanation only to confirm meaning.
What should we revisit if reading is a guess?
Return to the uncertain letter–sound link, model blending in order and try a different taught CVC word.

title: Use sounds and letters to spell
intro: I can hear the sounds in a word, choose taught spellings and read back what I wrote.
exampleTitle: One sound can use a letter team
example: Adult: say “fish”. Hear three sounds, then map f | i | sh. The two letters sh work together for the final sound, so the word has four letters but three phonemes. Read the spelling back to check that it says fish. Sound positions and written letters do not always have the same count.
steps: 1. Hear the whole word in order
Say the intended word naturally, then segment it. Keep every heard sound in order before writing. Supply familiar spoken meanings so vocabulary uncertainty does not become a spelling error.
Adult: say “bag”, meaning a container for carrying things. Keep its spelling hidden.
Say its sounds in order and choose the letters you know.
Bag uses b, a, g for the beginning, short middle vowel and final sound. A first-letter response alone does not spell the whole word.
2. Represent the vowel and any taught team
Choose the spelling taught for each sound position. A vowel can be easy to overlook; a known letter team can represent one sound. Use a fresh word after the model.
Adult: say “shop” without showing it. The learner already knows sh, o and p. Provide blank paper.
Write the word, then explain any team you used.
Shop: sh | o | p. The initial sh is one sound represented by two letters; the middle vowel is o. Read back the complete sequence to check.
3. Read back and keep meaningful parts
Read your own spelling as written and compare it with the intended word. Repair omissions or order errors. A familiar base can help when a meaningful ending is added.
Adult says “dogs”, meaning more than one dog. The learner writes dog. Show base dog and ending s after the attempt.
What needs to be added, and what meaning stays?

Add s to make dogs. The base dog keeps the animal meaning; the ending shows more than one here. In ordinary speech this s is voiced /z/. Check both the sounds represented and the familiar meaning part.
mistakes: “One sound always needs one letter.”
Sh in fish represents one sound with two letters.
“The right letters work in any order.”
Compare the written sequence with the intended spoken sequence.
“Only perfect adult spelling shows useful knowledge.”
Notice plausible use of taught correspondences, then explicitly teach the next convention.
activity: Adult: dictate “map”, then “fish”, one at a time without displaying them. The learner maps sounds, writes, and blends back. Ask what they would do if a sound were missing. Finally discuss dog and dogs with the printed base and ending.
adjust: Starter: supplied counters and two choices for one sound. Core: represent all sounds with taught letters or teams. Stretch: repair plan written as pan by locating the missing /l/, then explain a familiar plural ending.
safety: Dictate real speech and record which spellings have been taught. A plausible attempt is evidence of developing knowledge; distinguish it from fully conventional spelling and from copying a displayed answer.
tricky: 1. Does fish need four sound counters because it has four letters?
No. It has three phonemes; sh represents the last one.
2. For the intended word plan, is pan complete?
No. It misses /l/ after /p/. Put that sound and its l back before reading the word again.
3. Can s in dogs contribute meaning even though it is not a whole word?
Yes. It adds the more-than-one meaning in this example. A meaningful part need not stand alone as a word.
faq: Should adults correct every spelling in one turn?
Focus on the taught relationships and one useful next step. Ask the child to explain their choices before modelling a convention they do not yet know.
How can we check independent spelling fairly?
Say a fresh familiar word without revealing its spelling. Provide agreed access supports, record them and inspect every represented sound and any taught meaningful part.

title: Read and write familiar words
intro: I can read useful common words, check the whole word and write a word I have learnt.
exampleTitle: Connect sounds, meaning and the exact spelling
example: Read “The dog is on the rug.” Point to the. Adult: say it naturally and teach the th team and the vowel as pronounced in this sentence; the vowel may be the weak “uh” sound rather than a usual short-e sound. Notice the exact spelling t-h-e. Cover the model, write the word, uncover and compare every letter. Familiarity grows through meaningful reading and accurate sound–spelling attention, not outline guessing.
steps: 1. Read a taught common word
Look through the complete word and use the taught sound–spelling links. Some common words have an unusual or not-yet-taught part. An adult explains that part instead of asking for a guess.
Printed choices: and, my, is. Adult: read the sentence “The dog is here”, pointing to is, then revisit the word alone.
Which printed word was is? What did you check?
Is is i-s. Notice its vowel and the voiced final /z/ sound represented by s here. Compare the complete word with and and my, rather than choosing by its length alone.
2. Check the word in a sentence
Read the actual printed word, then check meaning and grammar in its sentence. Context helps confirm a reading; it does not replace looking at the letters.
Printed sentence: The cat is on my mat. Target cards: my / me.
Which card matches the word before mat? How does it fit the sentence?
My matches the printed m-y and tells whose mat it is. Me has a different final letter and does not fit this sentence position.
3. Write and compare a familiar word

Read a taught word and discuss its useful spelling features. Cover it, write it and check the full sequence. Personally familiar names are useful too, with their own exact spelling and capitalisation.
Printed model: go. Adult: read it, explain g and the o pronounced like its name here, then cover the model. Provide blank paper.
Write go, uncover the model and compare.
The word is g-o. Check both letters in order and reread it. Record whether the learner wrote from memory, copied or needed a prompt; those show different levels of support.
mistakes: “The first letter tells the whole word.”
Track to the end and compare every letter.
“Common words cannot use sound knowledge.”
Use known correspondences and explicitly teach unusual or new parts.
“Context lets me ignore print.”
Read the printed sequence and use context to confirm it.
activityTitle: One common word and one meaningful name
activity: Choose a taught common word such as my and a preferred name important to the learner. Supply their exact printed models, read them, discuss letters and sounds, then cover for a writing attempt. Uncover, compare and use each in a meaningful spoken sentence.
adjust: Starter: select and read one word beside a model. Core: read it in a sentence and write it after covering. Stretch: distinguish my from me in two supplied sentences: “This is my bag” and “Come with me.” Explain the final-letter difference.
safety: Use only some taught words at a time; no speed gate or exhaustive list is required. Names may have spellings from many languages. Check the preferred spelling with the learner or family rather than inventing a pronunciation rule.
tricky: 1. Is is spelt i-z because its last sound is /z/?
No. Its conventional spelling is i-s. Teach how s represents /z/ in this word.
2. Does the outside shape of the prove its spelling?
No. Check t-h-e in sequence and connect those letters with the spoken word.
3. If a child copied a name correctly, have they written it from memory?
No. Accurate copying is useful supported practice. Check recall separately after covering the model.
faq: Which words should we teach?
Choose useful high-frequency and personally familiar words that appear in current reading and writing. Revisit them meaningfully and teach their sound–spelling details.
What if the word has an unusual part?
Identify the known parts and explicitly model the new or unusual part. Return to the whole word in a clear sentence.

title: Find meaning inside words
intro: I can explain a whole word and notice parts that add to its meaning.
exampleTitle: A base word and a meaningful ending
example: Dog names an animal. Dogs keeps that base meaning and adds s to show more than one. Dog and s are two meaningful parts inside the one written word dogs. The s is not a separate word or a separate syllable here. Compare cup and cups to see the same more-than-one ending with a different base.
steps: 1. Begin with the whole word’s meaning
Say a word and connect it with something familiar. A word is a unit of meaning; the letters inside it help spell it, but each letter is not usually a separate meaning part.
Adult: place one cup on the table. Show the word cup and say it.
What does cup name? Does c alone mean a smaller cup?
Cup names the object used for drinking. The letters c, u and p help spell the word; they do not each name a separate part of its meaning.
2. Keep the base and add more-than-one
Compare one and more than one. Keep the familiar base and notice the ending that changes the number meaning. The ending can sound different across words while keeping its meaning.
Adult: place one cup on one side and three cups on the other. Show cup and cups.
Which word matches each group? What does the added s tell us?
Cup matches one; cups matches three. Cup keeps the object meaning and s adds more than one. In cups it is /s/; in dogs it is /z/. Do not use sound alone to decide whether a part carries meaning.
3. Join two familiar word meanings

Some familiar words combine two words. Explain how both meanings help with the whole word. A split is useful when the parts contribute meaning, not just because a group of letters happens to look like a word.
Printed parts: rain + coat → raincoat. Adult: show or draw a coat worn in rain and name it.
What does each part contribute? Is raincoat one word or two in print?
Rain tells the weather it is used for; coat names the clothing. Raincoat is one printed word built from two meaningful words. Do not confuse its two syllables with a general rule for meaning parts.
mistakes: “Every letter is a meaning part.”
Ask what meaning each proposed part contributes.
“Every word ending in s means more than one.”
Compare meaning: bus names one vehicle; its final s is part of the base.
“A word can be split anywhere.”
Choose a familiar base and ending or two words whose meanings explain the whole.
activityTitle: One, many and a word pair
activity: Use one spoon and several spoons. An adult supplies the printed words spoon and spoons, reads them and asks the learner to match meaning. Then supply sun and hat cards, join sunhat and explain a hat used in sunny conditions. Read and explain the complete word each time.
adjust: Starter: match one object and a group to named words. Core: identify the base and more-than-one s in a familiar pair. Stretch: compare cats with cat, then explain why bus does not split into bu plus plural s.
safety: An adult may read all words aloud; independent decoding is not required to explain meaning parts here. Use familiar objects or actual prepared pictures. Do not turn this introduction into a formal suffix taxonomy.
tricky: 1. Is dogs two words because dog and s have meanings?
No. Dogs is one word with two meaningful parts in this example.
2. Do cat and hat belong together because they share the base cat?
No. They rhyme, but hat does not contain the base cat. A shared sound ending is different from shared meaning.
3. Must every word have more than one meaningful part?
No. Cup is a useful simple base here; cups adds a number meaning. Only separate parts that make sense for the word being studied.
faq: Does plural s always sound the same?
No. It is /s/ in cats and /z/ in dogs in usual speech. The more-than-one meaning stays.
What should an adult listen for?
Ask the learner to explain the whole meaning, identify a sensible part and tell what it contributes. Saying a label such as ending without its meaning is not enough.
